title: Fall-risk-increasing drugs (FRIDs): CDC STEADI / STEADI-Rx, EuGMS STOPPFall and AGS Beers 2023 crosswalk
compiledBy: MedWatch research (UnivaBio hackathon); class lists transcribed from primary sources, deprescribing guidance paraphrased (not verbatim), brands verified via RxNorm/openFDA.

sources.citation: CDC STEADI. Medications Linked to Falls (fact sheet), 2017.

actions: REDUCE to the lowest effective dose
Develop a monitoring plan and use non-drug strategies
content.scope: Review prescription, OTC and herbal products for all patients 65+

sources.citation: CDC STEADI. SAFE Medication Review Framework (fact sheet), 2017.

steps: Screen for medications that may increase fall risk
Assess the patient to manage health conditions (goals, side effects, preferences, barriers)
Formulate a medication action plan (stop, switch, reduce, simplify, monitor)

sources.citation: CDC. Pharmacy Care (STEADI-Rx). Page updated Aug 3, 2025.
STEADI-Rx Community Pharmacy Fall Risk Checklist (UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy / CDC), 2019.

screeningQuestions: Any falls in the past year?
Feels unsteady when standing or walking?
Lightheadedness or dizziness from lying to standing?

sources.citation: STEADI-Rx: Older Adult Fall Prevention Guide for Community Pharmacists (CDC/UNC), 2020, 32 pp.

content.screenWho: Adults >=65 taking >=4 chronic medications or >=1 high-risk medication, or presenting with an acute fall; screen yearly.
content.orthostaticCheck: Lie down 5 minutes and measure BP; stand and re-measure at 1 and 3 minutes.
content.claimedEffect: The guide states that reducing medications whose risks outweigh benefits may reduce falls by 39-66% (citing Gillespie 2012 Cochrane and Pit 2007); this is CDC's summary, not independently re-checked here (UNVERIFIED).

sources.note: Template for pharmacist-to-prescriber communication: fall risk factors (falls in past year, worry, unsteadiness, orthostatic symptoms, >=4 chronic meds, >=1 high-risk med) + 'Medication Therapy Problem / Recommendation / Accept-Decline-Discuss'. Useful model for the MedWatch clinician brief.

sources.citation: Seppala LJ, Petrovic M, Ryg J, et al. STOPPFall (Screening Tool of Older Persons Prescriptions in older adults with high fall risk): a Delphi study by the EuGMS Task and Finish Group on Fall-Risk-Increasing Drugs. Age Ageing. 2021;50(4):1189-1199.
sources.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (per PMC record) - content here is paraphrased.

content.method: 3 Delphi rounds, 24 panellists from 13 European countries (2019-2020), 70% agreement threshold.
content.decisionTreesAppendix: Appendix IV-V of the article supplement (Europe PMC supplementary files)

sources.citation: 2023 American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria Update Expert Panel. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2023;71(7):2052-2081.

content.criterion: Drug-disease interaction: history of falls or fractures
content.recommendation: Avoid unless safer alternatives are not available; antiepileptics: avoid except for seizure and mood disorders; opioids: avoid except for pain management in severe acute pain. If one must be used, reduce other CNS-active drugs and use other fall-prevention strategies.
content.qualityOfEvidence: Antidepressants and opioids: moderate; all others: high

sources.citation: de Vries M, Seppala LJ, et al. JAMDA 2018;19:371.e1-9 (cardiovascular); Seppala LJ, et al. JAMDA 2018;19:371.e11-17 (psychotropics); Seppala LJ, et al. JAMDA 2018;19:372.e1-8 (others).
sources.note: The three meta-analyses that informed STOPPFall (cited as refs 2-4 in the STOPPFall paper); not re-read in this session.

sources.citation: NLM RxNav (RxNorm) REST API, queried 2026-10-10 for ingredient RxCUIs and brand -> ingredient verification.

considerWithdrawalIf: no current indication
a safer alternative exists
monitor: symptom change such as orthostatic hypotension, blurred vision, dizziness

engineGuidance.flagRule: Flag a medication as a FRID if it belongs to any class below; show which sources name the class (sourceCount) so the brief can say e.g. 'named by CDC STEADI and STOPPFall'.
engineGuidance.priorityHint: Classes named by >=3 sources (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, antipsychotics, opioids, antidepressants, antiepileptics) are the core psychoactive FRIDs; >=2 FRIDs or any FRID plus a reported fall/near-fall/dizziness is the strongest discussion prompt (MedWatch heuristic, not a validated score).
engineGuidance.steadiRxScreenTrigger: Per STEADI-Rx, screen when age >=65 and (>=4 chronic medications or >=1 high-risk medication) or an acute fall.
engineGuidance.noCausalClaims: FRID status is a population-level association; MedWatch must describe timing and counts only.

considerWithdrawalIf: daytime sedation, cognitive or psychomotor impairment
prescribed for sleep or anxiety
deprescribing.taperExample: Roughly 25% dose reduction every two weeks, with smaller (about 12.5%) steps near the end.

considerWithdrawalIf: daytime sedation, cognitive or psychomotor impairment
prescribed for sleep or anxiety
deprescribing.taperExample: STOPPFall groups Z-drugs with benzodiazepines (same decision tree): roughly 25% every two weeks, smaller steps near the end.

classes.name: Antipsychotics
subclassRiskNotes: Risk differs with each agent's sedative, anticholinergic and alpha-adrenergic blocking properties (STOPPFall Table 1).

considerWithdrawalIf: extrapyramidal or cardiac side effects, sedation, dizziness or blurred vision
prescribed for behavioural symptoms of dementia or for sleep (possibly bipolar disorder)
monitor: recurrence of psychosis, aggression, agitation, delusions or hallucinations
deprescribing.taperExample: For dementia-related behaviour treated >=3 months: reduce by 25-50% every 1-2 weeks.

classes.note: Prochlorperazine (often used as an antiemetic) is a phenothiazine dopamine antagonist; grouping it here is a MedWatch pharmacology-based assumption.

classes.name: Opioids
subclassRiskNotes: Strong opioids are more fall-risk-increasing than weak opioids (STOPPFall Table 1).

considerWithdrawalIf: slowed reactions, impaired balance or sedation
prescribed for chronic pain (possibly acute pain)
deprescribing.taperExample: Reduce by 5-25% of the daily dose every 1-4 weeks; faster if stopping for adverse effects, slower from high doses or long use.

classes.name: Antidepressants
subclassRiskNotes: Tricyclic antidepressants are more fall-risk-increasing than other antidepressants (STOPPFall Table 1).
Risk differs with sedation, propensity for orthostatic hypotension and anticholinergic activity (STOPPFall Table 1).
Beers 2023: evidence for falls/fractures is mixed for antidepressants; newer evidence suggests SNRIs may increase fall risk.

considerWithdrawalIf: hyponatraemia, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, sedation, or tachycardia/arrhythmia
prescribed for sleep; for depression depending on symptom-free time and history (possibly neuropathic pain or anxiety)
deprescribing.taperExample: Reduce by about 25% of the daily dose every 1-4 weeks.

classes.name: Antiepileptics (anticonvulsants)
subclassRiskNotes: Older-generation antiepileptics are more fall-risk-increasing than newer ones; risk differs with sedative effects (STOPPFall Table 1).
Beers 2023: avoid antiepileptics in people with falls/fractures except for seizure and mood disorders.

considerWithdrawalIf: ataxia, somnolence, impaired balance (possibly dizziness)
prescribed for anxiety or neuropathic pain

classes.note: Gabapentin and pregabalin are included as antiepileptics here (both are FDA-approved for seizures). Whether STOPPFall panellists meant them to be included is UNVERIFIED; their labels warn of dizziness and somnolence.

classes.name: Diuretics
subclassRiskNotes: Loop diuretics are more fall-risk-increasing than other diuretics (STOPPFall Table 1).

considerWithdrawalIf: orthostatic hypotension, hypotension or electrolyte disturbance (possibly urinary incontinence)
possibly when prescribed for hypertension
deprescribing.taperExample: Halve the dose at weekly intervals down to the lowest licensed dose, then stop.

considerWithdrawalIf: hypotension, orthostatic hypotension or dizziness

classes.name: Alpha-blockers for benign prostatic hyperplasia
subclassRiskNotes: Non-selective alpha-blockers are more fall-risk-increasing than selective ones (STOPPFall Table 1).

considerWithdrawalIf: hypotension, orthostatic hypotension or dizziness
deprescribing.taperExample: Can usually be stopped without a taper.

classes.name: Centrally-acting antihypertensives

considerWithdrawalIf: hypotension, orthostatic hypotension or sedation
deprescribing.taperExample: Taper over days to weeks depending on half-life (abrupt clonidine withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension - general pharmacology, not from STOPPFall).

classes.note: Moxonidine (also centrally acting) is not marketed in the US.

classes.name: Antihistamines (sedating / first-generation)
subclassRiskNotes: First-generation antihistamines are more fall-risk-increasing than second-generation; risk differs with sedation and anticholinergic activity (STOPPFall Table 1).

considerWithdrawalIf: confusion, drowsiness, dizziness or blurred vision
any indication (sleep/sedation, chronic itch, allergy)
deprescribing.taperExample: Reduce by 25-50% of the daily dose every 1-4 weeks.

classes.name: Vasodilators used in cardiac diseases (nitrates)

considerWithdrawalIf: hypotension, orthostatic hypotension or dizziness
deprescribing.taperExample: Gradual taper; panellists suggested keeping short-acting nitrate available while tapering.

classes.note: Mapping STOPPFall 'vasodilators used in cardiac diseases' to organic nitrates follows the WHO ATC group C01D (MedWatch interpretation).

classes.name: Medications for overactive bladder and urge incontinence

stoppFall.class: Overactive bladder and urge incontinence medications

subclassRiskNotes: Risk differs with anticholinergic activity (STOPPFall Table 1). Mirabegron/vibegron are beta-3 agonists without antimuscarinic action, so by that statement they would be expected to carry less anticholinergic-related risk (MedWatch inference, not a STOPPFall statement).

considerWithdrawalIf: dizziness, confusion, blurred vision, drowsiness or QT prolongation
deprescribing.taperExample: Reduce by 25-50% of the daily dose every 1-4 weeks.

classes.name: Anticholinergics (other strongly anticholinergic drugs)
subclassRiskNotes: Medications with high anticholinergic activity are more fall-risk-increasing than weak anticholinergics (STOPPFall Table 1). Use acb-scale.json (ACB >= 2) or Beers 2023 Table 7 to identify them.

classes.name: Skeletal muscle relaxants
classes.note: Listed by CDC STEADI (2017 fact sheet, 2020 STEADI-Rx guide) but not among the 14 STOPPFall classes and not among its 17 no-consensus classes.

classes.name: Other blood-pressure-lowering drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers)
subclassRiskNotes: STOPPFall reached NO consensus for ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers as FRIDs; CDC groups all 'medications affecting blood pressure' together. Flag only when dizziness/orthostatic symptoms or recent start/dose change co-occur (MedWatch design choice).

classes.name: Glucose-lowering drugs that can cause hypoglycaemia (sulfonylureas, insulin)
subclassRiskNotes: STOPPFall: oral hypoglycaemics as a class did NOT reach consensus, but panellists agreed that agents able to cause hypoglycaemia (sulfonylureas) are more fall-risk-increasing than other agents (Table 1).
